Peter Farrelly reveals why he made the difficult decision to move I Play Rocky's climactic Apollo Creed fight to the end credits, even after spending an entire week filming the sequence.

In this Collider interview, the director of I Play Rocky breaks down the challenges of recreating iconic moments from the original Rocky, including Sylvester Stallone's legendary run up the Philadelphia Museum of Art steps. Farrelly explains why the film's emotional high point ultimately mattered more than showcasing one of the production's most demanding sequences.

Farrelly also discusses working with cinematographer Sean Porter to match the original film's lighting and camera movements, including the decision to use green screen for the famous Philadelphia market scene where Rocky catches an orange.

One of the interview's most fascinating revelations involves Garrett Brown, the inventor of the Steadicam, who loaned the production his original equipment. Farrelly explains how Brown's technology helped inspire the original Rocky staircase sequence and how that filmmaking history became part of I Play Rocky.

The director also shares how conversations with Stallone influenced the movie's soundtrack, particularly the use of Buffalo Springfield, and why revisiting the original film revealed tiny details worth recreating.

She also discusses Episode 6's emotional mind-space sequences, the influence of WandaVision and Agatha All Along, and how films like Inception and Arrival helped inspire the series' balance of science fiction and human emotion.

In this Collider interview, Gray discusses the personal experiences that shaped Paper Tiger, his approach to directing Adam Driver, and why love is the driving force behind the film's characters.

Gray recalls witnessing a terrible argument between his parents and explains how he initially wrote a more dramatic version of the incident. But after rehearsing the scene, he realized the film needed something closer to the truth. He also shares how he helped Driver understand his character's motivations by emphasizing that even seemingly ordinary actions should come from love.

The filmmaker also breaks down his unusual writing process, revealing why he often develops a movie's ending first and works backward to establish its emotional journey.

One of the film's more surprising production details involves its driving sequences. Barker explains that the scenery outside the car windows was created using an LED wall rather than green screen or actual moving vehicles. Navarrette also discusses her extensive preparation for Nikki, including studying Toni Collette and Lupita Nyong'o and working closely with Barker to develop the character's physical movements. She explains how their collaboration gave her the freedom to explore the character while staying true to the director's vision.

Barker reflects on going from production assistant and COVID monitor to directing his own set, his mother's reaction to the movie, and the satisfaction of finally capturing the eerie, nostalgic feeling he wanted audiences to experience.

snippet.title: The Mosquito Bowl: Skarsgård Found Football Harder Than War | Set Stories
snippet.description:
The Mosquito Bowl: Why Football Was Harder Than War. Bill Skarsgård, Nicholas Galitzine, Tom Francis, and Ray Nicholson reveal how intense football training, chaotic battle sequences, and director Peter Berg's unconventional filmmaking approach shaped their performances in the 2026 war drama.

In this Collider interview, the cast of The Mosquito Bowl takes us behind the scenes of the physical and emotional challenges of portraying football players thrust into World War II. After spending a month in Australia training for hours each day in both football and military techniques, the actors discovered that recreating the sport could be even more demanding than filming combat.

Skarsgård discusses the challenge of convincingly playing an experienced American football player despite having only weeks to learn the game, while the cast reflects on navigating unpredictable battle scenes, muddy playing fields, and physically exhausting shoots.

The conversation also explores how Berg's spontaneous directing style encouraged the actors to embrace unexpected moments rather than rigidly follow a predetermined plan. From shooting with multiple handheld cameras to allowing performers to follow their instincts, the experience created an unusual sense of creative freedom.

The cast also opens up about the friendships they developed throughout production and how filming chronologically helped those relationships evolve naturally on screen.

snippet.title: A Talent for Murder: Alden's Nerdy Persona Was Meant to Fool You | Set Stories
snippet.description:
Helen Mirren, Alden Ehrenreich, and director Anton Corbijn reveal some of the stranger behind-the-scenes details from A Talent for Murder, including the production's unusually valuable snails and the animal wrangler tasked with handling them.

Speaking with Collider about the 2026 film, the cast and director discuss bringing Patricia Highsmith's world to the screen and how the story's ambiguity shaped their performances. Mirren explains why the script was so difficult to predict, while Corbijn shares how he approached directing experienced actors with very little rehearsal time.

Ehrenreich also reflects on the influence of The Talented Mr. Ripley and how Anthony Minghella's adaptation presented a more sympathetic version of Highsmith's famously slippery character. The conversation turns to the challenges of translating theatrical scenes into cinematic storytelling, including Corbijn's use of low camera angles and different positions within the central house.

Beyond the performances, the trio discusses filming locations, the movie's 1980s-inspired costumes, and the talented supporting cast.
But one of the funniest stories involves Highsmith's fascination with snails. The production had a snail wrangler, some surprisingly large snails, and a memorable joke that proves even the smallest performers can steal a scene.

snippet.title: The Cycle: A Rotting Throat Distorted the Werewolf’s Scream | Collider BTS
snippet.description:
Deborah Ann Woll had two major questions before agreeing to star in The Cycle: Would the monster effects be practical, and would director Jordan Downey be open to collaboration? The answers helped convince her to take on the role of Meg in the 2026 horror film.

In this Collider interview, Woll and Downey take us behind the scenes of The Cycle, exploring the practical creature effects, the unsettling monster design, and the creative decisions that shaped the film.
Downey explains why he didn't want to make a monster movie afraid to show its creature. Instead, he embraced a skeletal, asymmetrical, decaying design inspired by the monster's physical deterioration. Woll recalls seeing the effects work and realizing the artists had raised the bar for everyone involved.

The conversation also explores the forensic anthropology research behind Meg, including Woll's opportunity to speak with consultant Sue Black. She discusses how that preparation informed her performance and how she approaches fear without simply trying to act scared.
Plus, Woll shares why Downey's willingness to incorporate her script suggestions made this one of her most rewarding collaborations, while the director explains why the emotional tragedy behind a monster matters just as much as its appearance.

snippet.title: Treasure Island: 20 Years of Friendship Made Cruelty Harder | Set StoriesStories
snippet.description:
David Oyelowo went to extraordinary lengths to bring Long John Silver to life in Treasure Island, including a physically demanding transformation that took two months to recover from. Alongside Hayley Atwell, who plays Bess Hawkins, Oyelowo takes Collider behind the scenes of the 2026 television adaptation to discuss the practical effects, elaborate sets, and unexpected challenges of playing pirates.

To convincingly portray Long John Silver's missing leg, Oyelowo wore a restrictive brace that prevented his knee from bending, while a latex stump and green-screen techniques helped complete the illusion. The resulting hobble was so demanding that he needed two months to regain normal hip function.

Atwell also discusses how the production's practical sets, including a candlelit inn, helped create an immersive world that felt more authentic than working against a green screen. Oyelowo recalls the magic of filming the treasure discovery sequence and exploring Tenerife's striking landscapes.

The longtime friends also share some lighter moments from filming, including Atwell's attempts to recruit cast members for Bananagrams, their 20-year friendship, and how that history shaped their performances together.
